Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources gathered.

---

# Leviticus 15 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter deals with four types of bodily discharges that cause ceremonial uncleanness:
1. **Abnormal male discharge** (vv. 2–15) — likely a diseased condition of the genital organs
2. **Normal male emission of semen** (vv. 16–18)
3. **Normal female menstruation** (vv. 19–24)
4. **Abnormal female discharge of blood** (vv. 25–30)

The chapter closes with a summary (vv. 31–33). The key principle is given in v. 31: these laws were to keep Israel separate from uncleanness so that they would not die by defiling God's tabernacle.

**Central interpretive point, agreed across traditions:** These laws concern *ceremonial* purity, not *moral* purity. Normal bodily functions such as menstruation and marital intercourse are not sinful, but they rendered a person ritually unfit for worship at the sanctuary. As Precept Austin puts it, "There's nothing immoral about a husband and wife having sex or a woman having a period. The laws in Leviticus 15 governed ceremonial purity, not moral purity." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)

---

## Verse 1

**"And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron…"**

- **Ellicott** notes that this chapter "lays down the laws of uncleanness arising from issues" and discusses "two diseased and three natural secretions." The address to both Moses and Aaron is significant — Aaron and the priests would be responsible for administering these laws. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Precept Austin (Leon Hyatt)** suggests this message was "probably on the last of the days of fillings as a part of the hallowing ceremonies for the new priests." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)

---

## Verse 2

**"When any man has a bodily discharge, the discharge is unclean."**

- **Ellicott:** "Flesh, as is frequently the case, euphemistically denotes private parts." The phrase "his issue is unclean" means anyone coming in contact with it or with garments bearing traces of it is rendered unclean. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "The idea is of some obviously abnormal genital discharge, indicating some type of disease." Cites Rooker: "The exact nature of this discharge is not stated, although the most frequently suggested opinion is that it refers to gonorrhea." Notes that God deals with private matters "in an appropriate, dignified way." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-15/)
- **Calvin (Reformed):** Teaches that "men are defiled by the flow of the seminal fluid" — either involuntarily in sleep or through disease (gonorrhea). He sees this as a "general law for the cultivation of purity" not confined to chastity alone. Whatever proceeds from an unclean man is corrupt; no one can offer himself to God "except he who is pure and perfect in soul and body." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-15.html)
- **Precept Austin (KJV Bible Commentary):** "Whether this issue was sexual is not stated and should not necessarily be inferred. It could be any of a number of general issues, such as a discharge of blood, pus, or other fluid from a wound, lesion, boil, etc." Ryrie describes it as "a diseased condition of the male sexual organs resulting in bodily discharge." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)
- **Catholic (Haydock):** These legal uncleannesses "were instituted in order to give the people a horror of carnal impurities." Cites Challoner. Notes that if gonorrhea and the lawful act of marriage induce uncleanness, "surely to imitate Onan is most detestable." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-15.html)

---

## Verse 3

**"Whether his body allows the discharge to flow or blocks it. So his discharge will bring about uncleanness."**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Notes two ways of understanding the "blocked" discharge — either the discharge "may block the opening in the penis" (Peter-Contesse), or the condition is intermittent. The uncleanness persists regardless of whether it flows or is temporarily obstructed. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-15/)
- **Precept Austin (Hyatt):** "An intermittent discharge made a person unclean until it completely stopped. The person was unclean even in the periods of time between discharges. Until the discharge stopped altogether, the person remained unclean." Unlike leprosy (Lev 13–14), this uncleanness "did not have to be examined by a priest. The person was to recognize his uncleanness and act accordingly." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)
- **Calvin:** Observes that "uncleanness is contracted, not only when the seed is emitted, but when it is retained." This impressed upon Israel the seriousness of impurity, so that they might be "more accustomed to fly from all impurity." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-15.html)

---

## Verses 4–12: The Spread of Uncleanness from Abnormal Male Discharge

### v. 4 — Bed and furniture become unclean

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Essentially, the uncleanness associated with an abnormal genital discharge from a man was spread through contact. Therefore, it could be transmitted to a bed, to a place on which he sits, and by direct touch." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-15/)
- **Precept Austin (Hyatt):** Three actions were required to cleanse a person made unclean by contact: washing the clothes, bathing the body, and waiting until evening. This is more rigorous than cleansing from contact with an unclean creature (Lev 11), which required only washing clothes without bathing. "The lesson in the difference is that some sins are of such seriousness that additional effort is required to remove their effects." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)
- **Ellicott:** Notes the rabbinic tradition interpreted defilement by the bed in five different ways: "by standing, sitting, lying, hanging, or leaning on it." The patient's polluting power was considered so great "that even if the bed, seat, or saddle is under a stone, he defiles it through the stone." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)

### vv. 5–6 — Touching bed or furniture: wash clothes, bathe, unclean until evening

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Describes three levels of uncleanness: (1) the afflicted man himself; (2) objects or persons coming into direct contact with him; (3) someone who came in contact with an object made unclean on the second level. People and things on the second or third level could be purified by ceremonial washing and waiting until evening. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-15/)
- **F.B. Meyer (cited in Precept Austin):** "The unclean soul spreads uncleanness. Whatever the ceremonially unclean touched, used, or sat on, was polluted. Even those who came into contact with him were defiled. How wary all true Israelites must have been of their associates, lest they should contract pollution!" Spiritualizes it: "Let us adopt similar precautions, and not voluntarily associate with the unholy or unclean." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)

### v. 7 — Touching the body of the man with a discharge

- **Ellicott:** "With such intense loathing was the person regarded who had contracted this infirmity, that even the medical man who had professionally to examine him became defiled for the rest of the day." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)

### v. 8 — Spitting on someone who is clean

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "The uncleanness could also be spread through saliva. The general principle was that when the unclean comes into contact with the clean, it is the clean that is made unclean." Then notes the gospel reversal: "When Jesus – who was 'clean' in every sense – touched an unclean person, He made them clean (Luke 5:12-14). They didn't make Him unclean." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-15/)
- **Ellicott:** "Spitting in the face of a person was, and still is, commonly resorted to among Oriental nations as an expression of insult and contempt." The patient, being more irritable from the disease, would be "liable to give vent more frequently to this mode of expressing his wrath." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)

### v. 9 — Saddle/riding gear becomes unclean

- **Ellicott:** The Hebrew word translated "saddle" only occurs twice more in Scripture. It likely denotes "the well-known palanquin so largely used in the East" — a carriage or litter carried by men (as in Song of Solomon 3:10). Notes that the LXX adds "until evening," which has probably "dropped out of the Hebrew text." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Precept Austin (KJV note):** The word *merchav* "rather means a litter, or coune." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)

### v. 10 — Touching or carrying what was under him

- **Ellicott:** "Whoso carries the palanquin, with the patient in it, from one place to another, contracts defilement." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)

### v. 11 — Touching without rinsing hands

- **Ellicott:** If the patient touches anyone "with his hands without having first washed his hands," the touched person contracts pollution. "This is the only instance where the touch of the hand as imparting defilement is expressly mentioned, and where the washing of the hands alone is ordered in the Mosaic Law to prevent the communication of pollution." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Precept Austin** notes debate over whether "hath not rinsed his hands" refers to the diseased man or to the one touched. The Syriac refers it to the person touched, "though it seems strange that he should be cleansed by washing his hands, when perhaps some other part was touched." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)

### v. 12 — Clay pots broken, wooden utensils rinsed

- **Ellicott:** Clay vessels must be destroyed because they are porous and uncleanness penetrates (cf. Lev 6:28; 11:33). "This, however, is the only instance where an earthen vessel touched on the outside was defiled, thus again showing the intense loathing with which the guilt of this kind of infirmity was regarded." Wooden vessels are spared and rinsed — the Law "mercifully spares the more costly utensils." Notes that rabbinic tradition extended "wood" to include metal vessels, and orthodox Jews to this day "literally baptize cups, plates, knives, forks, or any new utensil which they buy" (referenced in Mark 7:4). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Precept Austin (Hyatt):** "The reason was that clay vessels were porous, and the uncleanness could penetrate into them. A wooden vessel, which uncleanness would not penetrate, was to be washed in water." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)

---

## Verses 13–15: Cleansing from Abnormal Male Discharge

### v. 13 — Seven days, wash clothes, bathe in fresh/running water

- **Gill (Baptist):** "When he that hath an issue is cleansed of his issue" means "it is ceased from him." Jarchi notes these must be "seven pure days, quite free from pollution, and continued in a constant course, without interruption." Gersom adds that if any impurity appeared during any of these days, the count restarted. Maimonides said "he must begin to number again from the day of the last appearance." Gill sees the "running water" as "typical of the fountain opened in Christ to wash in for sin and uncleanness, even the fountain of his blood, which cleanses from all sin." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/15.htm)
- **Ellicott:** "Bathe his flesh in running water" — literally "living water." Unlike all other defiled persons (who could use collected water), "the restored man who had suffered from the issue in question was ordered to bathe in a fountain or in spring water." Suggests "flesh" here is again a euphemism for the genital area, noting that when the whole body is meant, the text adds "all" (as in v. 16). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Precept Austin (KJV Bible Commentary):** "After the issue was healed, seven days were counted; and then the ceremonial bathing was performed." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)

### v. 14 — On the eighth day, two turtledoves or young pigeons

- **Ellicott:** It is "very striking that whilst in other cases it was only the poor who, out of consideration, were allowed two turtledoves or two young pigeons… in the case before us the meanest offering was prescribed for all alike who suffered from this infirmity, without giving them the choice of bringing a more costly sacrifice." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)

### v. 15 — One as sin offering, one as burnt offering; atonement made

- **Ellicott:** The atonement is "for the sinful act which has brought about the infirmity." Notes the severity of treatment: those with this disease had to remain outside the camp (Numbers 5:1-4), and during the Second Temple were "debarred from partaking of the Paschal meal, and were banished from the precincts of the holy city." David's imprecation in 2 Samuel 3:29 reflects this: "Let there not fail from the house of Joab one that hath an issue." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Catholic (Haydock/Du Hamel):** "For sin. Legal, or any other that he may have incurred." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-15.html)

---

## Verses 16–18: Normal Male Discharge (Emission of Semen)

### v. 16 — Bathe whole body, unclean until evening

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The fact that even normal, permitted sexual activity made a man ceremonially unclean "was not God's condemnation of sex. It was a powerful way to prevent an aspect of sexual and spiritual corruption common in the ancient world: ritual prostitution, often practiced at a sacred place." Cites Rooker: "The declaration of semen as unclean in this passage illustrates the sharp distinction between Israelite religion and the pagan religions of the ancient Near East. In pagan religion sexual activity among worshipers was believed to activate the gods into fertilizing the soil with rain." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-15/)
- **Ellicott:** This is the case of "an involuntary emission, as in Deuteronomy 23:10." Notes parallels: "the Egyptian priests when they were defiled by a dream purified themselves by bathing their bodies; and, according to the directions of the Koran, any faithful Mahommedan who meets with such an accident must not perform his prayers till he has gone through the prescribed oblation." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Catholic (Menochius, via Haydock):** Notes this could refer to "nocturnal inconveniences" (v. 16) while v. 18 deals with the act of marriage. The uncleanness from marriage "rendered unclean only in as much as it hindered a person from partaking of any thing sacred, though he might perform the duties of life." Adds (Theodoret/Du Hamel): "This law was to lay some restraint on the too frequent use of marriage." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Calvin (Reformed):** Notes that even someone "who was conscious of no sin in the seminal-flux" was "reminded by this sign of the corruption of his nature" — corruption cleaves to the whole human race. The ablution points to Christ who came "by water and blood" to purge all uncleanness (1 John 5:6). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-15.html)

### v. 17 — Clothing or leather with semen must be washed, unclean until evening

- **Ellicott:** "Every skin" means everything made of skin (leather), in distinction from ordinary garments of fabric. "It is from this circumstance that the apostle borrows the expression 'hating even the garments spotted by the flesh' (Jude 1:23)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)

### v. 18 — Man and woman after intercourse: both bathe, unclean until evening

- **Ellicott:** "Even when what is specified in Leviticus 15:16 takes place in intercourse between man and woman lawfully married, it pollutes both the husband and the wife." Notes that "abstinence from conjugal intercourse was regarded as a necessary preparation for the performance of sacred duties" (cf. Exodus 19:15; 1 Samuel 21:5-6). "The law of pollution was not designed to put a check upon marriage, since matrimony is a Divine institution… but it is intended to prevent husband and wife from making an immoderate use of their conjugal life." Cites parallels among Hindoos, Babylonians, and Egyptian priests. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "It is the habit of many today – even many believers – to consider their sexual life and practices to be their own business and not God's business. Here we see that God has a part in even natural, permitted, blessed expressions of sexuality." Cites F.B. Meyer: "We must bring the thought of God into the simplest, the commonest, and the most secret acts. Nothing is outside His jurisdiction." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-15/)

---

## Verses 19–24: Normal Female Menstruation

### v. 19 — Seven days unclean; anyone touching her unclean until evening

- **Gill (Baptist):** "Her issue in her flesh be blood" distinguishes this from bleeding elsewhere (e.g., nosebleed). "She shall be put apart seven days" — "not out of the camp, nor out of the house, but might not go into the house of God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/15-19.html)
- **Ellicott:** Though the discharge usually ceases after three or four days, the period is extended to seven "to include exceptional cases" (cf. Lev 12:2). Notes the merciful contrast with pagan customs: ancient superstitions held that a menstruating woman could cause fruit to fall from trees, blunt tools, or sour meat. "The Parsees not only isolated her from the rest of the family, but forbade her speaking to any one." By contrast, the Mosaic Law gave "benign and necessary rules" that restrained such superstitions and inhumanity. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Notes an additional benefit: "The laws would also provide the woman a break from housework, caring for children, and marital relations" (Rooker). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-15/)
- **Calvin (Reformed):** "In every shameful thing the Jews were reminded of their uncleanness, that thus they might be accustomed to modesty and seek after purity." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-15.html)

### vv. 20–23 — Beds, furniture, and indirect contact all transmit uncleanness

- **Ellicott (v. 23):** Distinguishes between primary and secondary defilement. Verses 21–22 deal with touching the bed or seat itself (requiring washing clothes, bathing, and waiting until evening). Verse 23 deals with touching "any vessel, garment, or any other objects which are lying on the defiling bed or seat" — this is secondary pollution, requiring only waiting until evening "without having to wash his garments." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)

### v. 24 — If a man lies with her during menstruation, he is unclean seven days

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** "A man who had sex with a woman during her days of normal menstruation was also unclean seven days, following the course of the woman's uncleanness." Notes that "avoidance of intercourse during menstruation was later mentioned in Ezekiel 18:6 as an evidence of a righteous man." Stresses that "under the New Covenant this is no longer binding on Christians," but the principle of sexual restraint remains universal. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-15/)
- **Ellicott:** Notes that committing this act *presumptuously* carried the death penalty (Lev 18:19; 20:18). The seven-day uncleanness here applies when done in ignorance. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Catholic (Haydock):** "Supposing the case was not brought before the judge, and the man did it through ignorance: otherwise it was death, chap. xx. 18." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-15.html)

---

## Verses 25–27: Abnormal Female Discharge (Beyond Normal Menstruation)

### v. 25 — Discharge for many days outside normal period

- **Ellicott:** "This is the kind of complaint from which the woman suffered who came to Christ (Matthew 9:20; Luke 8:44). As long as she suffered from it, which lasted sometimes for many years, she defiled and was defiling in the same way as in her menses." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** This is "the fifth case of an issue—that of excessive menstruation, or menstruation occurring at the wrong time. This was probably the disease of the woman 'who had an issue of blood.'" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Precept Austin (Moody Bible/Today in the Word):** This condition is called "menostaxis" — "a chronic hemorrhage." Notes that the woman Jesus healed in Mark 5 suffered from this. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)

### vv. 26–27 — Same rules as for normal menstruation regarding beds, furniture, and contact

- **Ellicott:** "The rules here laid down about her defilement and defiling are the same as those in Leviticus 15:20-22." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)

---

## Verses 28–30: Cleansing for Abnormal Female Discharge

### v. 28 — When cleansed, count seven days, then ceremonially clean

- **Ellicott:** "'Cleansed' is used both here and in Leviticus 15:13 for the disappearance of the complaint. From the time of its cessation she is to count seven days, during which no trace of the complaint must be observable, just as in the case of the less innocent disorder." Notes she becomes clean "after having performed the rites of lustration." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)

### vv. 29–30 — Two turtledoves or pigeons, sin offering and burnt offering

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** This is "the same procedure followed after the cleansing of a man with an abnormal genital discharge." Cites Rooker: "The reason offerings had to be made for these discharges and not for the discharges of semen and menstruation was because they were considered abnormal." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-15/)
- **Ellicott:** She brings "the same sacrifices which are prescribed for the man who is cured of an issue (see Leviticus 15:14), only that in the latter case the man had to be bathed in living water, because he brought the illness upon himself." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Clarke (Methodist):** "In all these cases moral pollution was ever considered as being less or more present, as even such infirmities sprang from the original defection of man. On these accounts sacrifices must be offered." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/leviticus/15.htm)

---

## Verses 31–33: Summary and Purpose

### v. 31 — Keep Israel separate from uncleanness, lest they die defiling the tabernacle

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "The main purpose in the laws of uncleanness is to keep first God's house and then God's people free from the danger of defilement by foul things presenting themselves freely before him and among them. These foul things, symbolizing sinful things, create a ceremonial defilement symbolizing moral defilement." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-15.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Repeats the key point: "None of these discharges made a man or a woman sinful, only ceremonially unclean." Normal discharges were connected with "symbols of redemption and life, blood and semen." The message is "that there is something broken and inherently impure in us, even in what comes from us normally." Also notes separation of sex from worship: "To the modern world this seems normal, but in the ancient world it was common to worship the gods by having sex with temple prostitutes." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-15/)
- **Calvin (Reformed):** "God, I say, briefly sets forth His intention that He would drive away all profanation far from His people; because he desires sincerity to prevail amongst his worshippers, and cannot bear his tabernacle to be polluted by any stain." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-15.html)
- **Precept Austin:** "The tabernacle was a sacred place—the place where the people would meet with God—and the Israelites were to approach God with the utmost veneration and respect." The rules remind the people "that they are flesh and God is spirit; that they carry a personal pollution even when they do not sin outright; that they are privileged to be set apart by God and invited to His tabernacle; and that what happens in secret is seen by God." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)
- **Clarke (Methodist):** "By this separation the cause became less frequent, and the contagion, if it did exist, was prevented from spreading. So pest-houses and fever-wards are constructed for the purpose of separating the infected from the sound." Also warns that one "may not presume to enter into the tabernacle of God till purified, lest he provoke Divine justice to consume him, while attempting to worship with a polluted mind and impure hands." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/leviticus/15.htm)
- **Haydock (Catholic):** God "threatens to kill them, if they approach unclean." Jerome (in Gal. v.) understands this of "those abominable sins, which ought not to be mentioned." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-15.html)

### vv. 32–33 — Summary of the law

- **Precept Austin (KJV Bible Commentary):** "These verses restate the nature of this chapter. It is to teach and impose a ceremonial uncleanness for certain bodily discharges. These are no longer in force in the New Testament." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Points to the New Testament perspective: Jesus criticized the Pharisees for over-emphasizing ceremonial cleanliness while neglecting internal cleanliness (Mark 7:1-9). In Acts 15, the early church discerned "that under the New Covenant, the believer was not bound to these laws of ritual purity." Yet "spiritual cleanliness in worship is important today" — our cleansing comes through abiding in Christ (John 15:3; 1 John 1:7-9). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-15/)

---

## Denominational Distinctives and Differing Emphases

### Reformed (Calvin)
Calvin emphasizes that even involuntary bodily discharges point to the corruption of human nature after the Fall. "He who was conscious of no sin in the seminal-flux, still must be reminded by this sign of the corruption of his nature." The ceremonial law serves as a "schoolmaster" driving people to seek purification in Christ. Calvin explicitly ties the water of purification to 1 John 5:6 — "Christ came 'by water and blood,' to purge and expiate all uncleanness." The sacrifice of Christ is the reality behind the turtle-dove offerings. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-15.html)

### Baptist (Gill)
Gill's approach is characteristically Christ-centered and typological. The "running water" for bathing is "typical of the fountain opened in Christ to wash in for sin and uncleanness, even the fountain of his blood, which cleanses from all sin; and in which both the persons and garments of the saints are washed and made white." Gill draws heavily on rabbinic sources (Jarchi, Gersom, Maimonides) for the technical details of the seven-day waiting period. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/leviticus/15.htm)

### Methodist/Wesleyan (Clarke)
Clarke emphasizes both the sanitary/hygienic wisdom of the laws and their spiritual meaning. He notes the practical benefit: "By this separation the cause became less frequent, and the contagion, if it did exist, was prevented from spreading." Yet he also stresses that "God has purity of heart continually in view — that the soul may be holy, he cuts off the occasions of sin; and that men may be obliged to keep within due bounds, and possess their vessels in sanctification and honor, he hedges up their way with briars and thorns, and renders transgression painful, shameful, and expensive." He pointedly adds that these chapters, "avoided and neglected by most, contain lessons of instruction for all" and are "highly necessary to be known." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/leviticus/15.htm)

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Guzik emphasizes the contrast between the Old Covenant principle ("uncleanness spreads from unclean to clean") and the New Covenant reversal in Jesus ("the Clean touches the unclean and makes them clean"). He highlights the practical separation of sex from worship that these laws created: Israel was radically distinct from pagan fertility cults where ritual prostitution was common. He also stresses New Testament freedom: "under the New Covenant, the believer was not bound to these laws of ritual purity" (Acts 15), while still maintaining that spiritual cleanliness matters. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-15/)

### Anglican (Ellicott)
Ellicott provides the most detailed philological and historical analysis. He carefully distinguishes the Hebrew terms, notes where the LXX differs from the Masoretic text (e.g., the missing "until evening" in v. 9), and draws extensively on comparative ancient Near Eastern and rabbinic practice. His tone is measured and scholarly. He is notably the only commentator to note that the man with an abnormal discharge was required to bathe in "living water" (spring water) while all other defiled persons could use collected water — and that this higher requirement was "because he brought the illness upon himself." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-15.html)

## Catholic and Orthodox Readings

### Catholic (Haydock / Challoner)
The Catholic reading, following Challoner (18th century), sees these laws as given "in order to give the people a horror of carnal impurities." Haydock draws practical moral applications: if even lawful marital intercourse and involuntary emissions cause ceremonial uncleanness, willful sexual sins are all the more detestable. The note on v. 24 makes an important canonical distinction: intercourse during menstruation done in ignorance brought seven days' uncleanness, but done knowingly incurred the death penalty (Lev 20:18). The Catholic Douay-Rheims rendering of v. 15 reads "he shall pray for him before the Lord, that he may be cleansed of the issue of his seed" — emphasizing the priest's intercessory role. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-15.html)

## Modern Scholarship and Other Views

While the search for bibleodyssey.org and netbible.org did not return Leviticus 15-specific results within the search limits, some modern scholarly insights appear in the commentaries above:

- **Dr. Constable's Expository Notes** (as excerpted in search results): Notes that the uncleanness from these discharges "was less serious ritually than those associated with skin disease. The man could live at home; he did not need to move outside the camp." Also observes that "what made these secretions unclean was perhaps their association with unnatural (irregular) bodily functions" — not because sex is sinful. Cites Wenham: "The sexual processes thus make men and women unclean, but that is not the same as saying they are sinful." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-15.html)

- **Precept Austin (Leon Hyatt)** pushes back against common assumptions: "It is wrong to immediately assume that the first type of discharge was gonorrhea or some other kind of sexually transmitted disease, as many have done. Many conditions can cause abnormal discharges from the genital organs." Also critiques those who call normal discharges "foul" or "repulsive" as revealing "a negative, even unhealthy attitude toward the normal, God-given processes of reproduction." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)

- **TODAY IN THE WORD (Moody Bible)** suggests that for the sin and burnt offerings required after abnormal discharges, "it may be better to think in terms of purification rather than atonement" — a significant nuance. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_15_commentary)

## Summary of Key New Testament Connections (Across Traditions)

1. **The woman with the issue of blood** (Mark 5:25–34; Matt 9:20; Luke 8:44) — she suffered from the condition described in Lev 15:25–30. Her touch of Jesus' garment, which should have made Him unclean under the law, instead brought her healing. This illustrates the gospel reversal: Jesus' purity overcomes impurity.

2. **Acts 15** — The Jerusalem Council determined Gentile believers were not bound by Mosaic ceremonial laws, including the purity regulations of Leviticus 15.

3. **Mark 7:1–9** — Jesus criticized Pharisees for elevating ceremonial washing above internal purity.

4. **1 John 1:7–9** — "The blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanses us from all sin." Under the New Covenant, cleansing comes through Christ's blood, not ritual water.

5. **2 Corinthians 7:1** — Calvin ties this to Leviticus 15: Paul exhorts believers to "cleanse themselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit."
